name: Light Heliotrope-Grey
lede: Light Heliotrope-Grey lightens [[heliotrope-grey]], a flower-named grey-purple, and is Claude Monet's single favorite shade of its kind in our archive.

sections.title: A paled grey-purple
sections.body: The name is the modifier *light* set against the base color [[heliotrope-grey]], itself named for the pale purple heliotrope flower [1]. Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Nomenclature* records the matching range on plate L, hue 65'''', tone f, a scan of an aged plate and so an approximation [1]. The ISCC-NBS lists of 1955 file the same block as 227, "light purplish gray," a Delta-E of 4.8 away [1]. Nearest on file is [[black-shadows]] at 3.2 units, with [[mauve-grey]] and [[mauve-grey]] both at 4.2 [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this shade, as photographed, in 177 of 23,781 paintings, 0.74 percent; within a single canvas it is a distinct area in 109 of them, more common than 60 percent of our named colors [2]. Claude Monet is its most devoted painter, using it in 6 of 50 works here, 9.2 times the baseline rate of the museums those paintings come from [2]. It peaks in the 1900s at 1.7 percent of that century's 1,674 paintings, 2.7 times the expected rate, and inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 61 percent of its 109 appearances [2]. The earliest match dates to 1119, 793 years before the name's 1912 record; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first [2]. It is also most over-represented in Swedish paintings in our data, 3.7 times expected [2].
